newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - FX vols steady, eyes on curve flattening.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FX vols steady, eyes on curve flattening.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar-pair options were steady in late U.S. trade as the market awaited Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee meeting, dealers said.

Activity focussed on position adjustments and spread trading as few traders were willing to take on positions aggressively. A market holiday in Japan overnight and the Yom Kippur holiday also subdued trading.
One-month implied volatilities for dollar/mark and dollar/yen stood at 6.60/6.80 and 6.70/6.85 percent, respectively.

"This seems to have become their new home in the last month," said Alan Revercomb, options strategist at I.D.E.A. Inc. "Six and a half percent is a kind of roosting place where they wait (for market-moving events)."

While there was a fair amount of interest in shorter dated options, as some traders sought gamma ahead of FOMC, skeptics said volatilities might not pick up much whether or not the Fed raised interest rates.
Revercomb said major economic releases and Fed meetings this year have usually been a letdown from an implied volatility standpoint.
"It just hasn't really paid to take those kind of positions," he said.
Still, Masao Okada, chief options dealer at Dai-ichi Kangyo Bank in New York, said volatilities could be less prone to the usual post-event sell-off this time around.
"We haven't seen volatilities being pumped up too much beforehand, so the drop-off could be limited," he said.
Okada added that the market could move into a fresh phase after the FOMC, where the spot dollar would trade above 110 yen and volatilities would be more sensitive to the dollar's upside.
He said this could prompt traders to unwind the recent steepening in the volatility curve.

Longer-dated dollar/yen volatilities tended to rise relative to the shorter maturities when perception of risk was focussed on the dollar's downside, he noted. This was because of the differences in actual at-the-money strike prices stemming from the steep discount in forward points.
"I wouldn't be surprised if the very short-dated options stay subdued," Okada said. "But the spreads between the three-, six-month area and the one-year area seem too steep."
Revercomb at I.D.E.A. agreed that volatility spreads were likely to start tightening soon.
"The back end has been pretty stubborn in staying up because there has been some periodic interest," Revercomb said. "But the longer we stay here, the harder it's going to be to sustain that."

Traders also noted that seasonal factors were distorting the curve. Bidding was weak in the three-month area because three-month options traded today would expire on December 24, usually the market's most inactive time of the year. -Derivatives Desk 312-408-8750 E-mail: derivatives@reuters.com
